sections.title: The letter Ypsilon
paragraphs: The German letter (Ypsilon) /ʏpsilɔn/ mostly makes the sound /j/, as in (Yoga) /ˈjoːɡa/, which means yoga. This letter makes four sounds in total.

sections.title: Making the sounds
paragraphs: For the first sound, push your tongue high and forward while pursing your lips into a tight circle. For the second sound, relax your tongue slightly and keep your lips in a loose circle. For the third sound, raise your tongue near your roof and let air glide smoothly past. For the fourth sound, spread your lips wide and raise your tongue high. Touch your throat to feel your voice buzz for each one.

sections.title: Reading the letter
paragraphs: In stressed open parts of Greek loanwords, it makes the sound /yː/, that is a long tight ue sound, as in (Typ) /tyːp/. In closed parts of Greek loanwords, it makes the sound /ʏ/, that is a short loose ue sound, as in (System) /zʏsˈteːm/. Before vowels in modern loanwords, it makes the sound /j/, as in (Yacht) /jaxt/. At the end of words or unstressed syllables, it makes the sound /i/, as in (Handy) /ˈhɛndi/.

sections.title: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not pronounce Greek words with the flat vowel in bit or the glide in use. Purse your lips firmly into a circle while saying see. Do not change your lip shape while the vowel rings out.
